title: Pond
description: A small body of freshwater that provides a home for a huge variety of life.
climate: Temperate, experiencing four distinct seasons. Ponds create their own microclimate (a tiny, specific climate zone) that can freeze in winter and become very warm in summer.
plants: Water lilies, duckweed, reeds, and bulrushes which provide oxygen and shelter. They also rely on phytoplankton (microscopic floating plants) to feed tiny creatures.
fun_facts: A single pond can support over 1,000 different species of animals!
Unlike a fast-moving river, a pond's still water allows delicate insects like pond skaters to literally walk on the water's surface.
image_caption: A Common frog (Rana temporaria) in its natural habitat: Pond.

animals.name: Common frog (Rana temporaria)
animals.how_it_survives: Frogs lay their jelly-like eggs (spawn) in the still water. The tadpoles grow underwater before developing legs to hop onto land.

animals.name: Great diving beetle
animals.how_it_survives: Breathes underwater by trapping a bubble of air under its wing cases.

animals.name: Smooth newt
animals.how_it_survives: Can absorb oxygen directly through its moist skin while underwater.

title: Woodland
description: An area of land covered with trees, providing a rich and varied environment for wildlife with multiple layers (canopy to floor).
climate: Temperate with moderate rainfall. The tree canopy provides shade, keeping the forest floor cool, damp, and protected from harsh sun.
plants: Oak, ash, and beech trees, alongside bluebells, ferns, and mosses.
fun_facts: Trees in a woodland communicate and share nutrients through a vast underground fungal network known as the 'Wood Wide Web'.
Woodlands change completely depending on the season: in spring they are bursting with wildflowers, but in winter they look entirely asleep as deciduous trees drop their leaves.
image_caption: A Woodpecker in its natural habitat: Woodland.

animals.name: Woodpecker
animals.how_it_survives: Uses its long, sticky tongue to pull insects out of holes it drills in tree bark. Nests safely high up in tree trunks.

animals.name: Eurasian badger
animals.how_it_survives: Digs complex underground tunnel systems called setts to stay safe and warm.

animals.name: Tawny owl
animals.how_it_survives: Has specialized feathers with soft edges for completely silent flight to catch prey in the dark.

title: Hedgerow
description: A line of bushes and trees that acts as a boundary for a field, creating a safe wildlife corridor.
climate: Temperate. Hedgerows create microclimates (small pockets of unique weather), acting as windbreaks and retaining moisture in the soil.
plants: Hawthorn, blackthorn, brambles, and wild roses.
fun_facts: Hedgerows in the UK are often hundreds of years old and act as vital 'highways' for wildlife to travel safely between habitats.
A single thick hedgerow can be home to nesting birds, hibernating hedgehogs, and thousands of insects all at the same time.
image_caption: A Hazel dormouse (Muscardinus avellanarius) in its natural habitat: Hedgerow.

animals.name: Hazel dormouse (Muscardinus avellanarius)
animals.how_it_survives: Uses the continuous line of branches to travel safely above ground, finding berries and nuts without being seen by predators.

animals.name: European hedgehog
animals.how_it_survives: Rolls into a tight ball of sharp spines to protect itself from predators.

animals.name: Yellowhammer
animals.how_it_survives: Builds well-hidden cup nests deep within the thorny brambles to keep its chicks safe.

title: Dead Log
description: A fallen tree trunk or branch that is slowly rotting away on the woodland floor.
climate: Damp and shaded microclimate (a tiny localized climate), insulated from extreme temperature changes.
plants: Fungi, lichens, and mosses that thrive on decaying wood.
fun_facts: A dead log is teeming with more life than a living tree, hosting thousands of detritivores (creatures that eat dead matter) that recycle nutrients back into the soil.
Woodlice and millipedes love the dark, damp conditions under the bark, where they are protected from birds and the drying sun.
image_caption: A Stag beetle (Lucanus cervus) in its natural habitat: Dead Log.

animals.name: Stag beetle (Lucanus cervus)
animals.how_it_survives: The larvae spend several years living inside the dead wood, eating the rotting timber until they are ready to emerge as adult beetles.

animals.name: Woodlouse
animals.how_it_survives: Has a tough segmented exoskeleton and thrives in the damp, dark microclimate of rotting wood.

animals.name: Centipede
animals.how_it_survives: A fast predator that hunts smaller insects and grubs hiding in the crevices of the dead log.

title: Oak Tree
description: A single large tree that acts as a massive high-rise home for over 500 different species.
climate: Temperate. The tree itself creates various microclimates (tiny climate zones) from its sunny, breezy canopy down to its shaded, damp roots.
plants: The oak tree itself, plus epiphytes (plants that grow on other plants) like moss and lichens growing on its bark.
fun_facts: A mature oak tree can support over 280 species of insects, making it a crucial hub of biodiversity.
Squirrels and jays bury acorns from oak trees to eat later, but they often forget them, which is exactly how new oak forests are planted!
image_caption: A Purple hairstreak butterfly (Favonius quercus) in its natural habitat: Oak Tree.

animals.name: Purple hairstreak butterfly (Favonius quercus)
animals.how_it_survives: Spends almost its entire life high in the oak canopy. The caterpillars feed exclusively on oak leaves.

animals.name: Eurasian jay
animals.how_it_survives: Caches (buries) thousands of acorns in the ground for winter food, helping plant new oak trees.

animals.name: Gall wasp
animals.how_it_survives: Lays eggs in oak leaves, causing the tree to grow protective round 'galls' that shelter the growing larvae.

title: Arctic Sea Ice
description: The frozen surface of the Arctic Ocean, which expands in winter and shrinks in summer.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Hot and cold areas of the world

climate: Extreme polar climate, with temperatures dropping well below -30°C in winter and experiencing months of total darkness.
plants: Ice algae that grow on the underside of the sea ice, forming the base of the food web.
fun_facts: Arctic sea ice shrinks in the summer and expands in the winter, acting like a giant, pulsing white mirror that reflects sunlight and cools the Earth.
Unlike a penguin (which lives in the Antarctic), a polar bear's fur is actually hollow and transparent—it only looks white because it reflects the snow!
image_caption: A Polar Bear (Ursus maritimus) in its natural habitat: Arctic Sea Ice.

animals.name: Polar Bear (Ursus maritimus)
animals.how_it_survives: Uses the vast ice floes as a platform to hunt seals when they surface to breathe. Thick blubber and hollow hair keep it warm.

animals.name: Ringed seal
animals.how_it_survives: Uses strong claws to scratch and keep breathing holes open in the thick ice all winter.

animals.name: Arctic fox
animals.how_it_survives: Often follows polar bears out onto the sea ice to scavenge leftover food during the harsh winter.

title: Arctic Tundra
description: A vast, flat, treeless region where the subsoil is permanently frozen (permafrost).
climate: Extremely cold, dry, and windy. It features a layer of permanently frozen soil called permafrost (ground that never thaws).
plants: Dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, mosses, and lichens. Trees cannot grow here because the permafrost prevents deep roots.
fun_facts: During the short Arctic summer, the tundra bursts into life with millions of migratory birds and blooming wildflowers.
Compared to an urban red fox in England, the Arctic Fox has much shorter ears and a rounder body to prevent heat from escaping into the freezing air.
image_caption: A Arctic Fox (Vulpes lagopus) in its natural habitat: Arctic Tundra.

animals.name: Arctic Fox (Vulpes lagopus)
animals.how_it_survives: Changes its coat colour from brown in summer to thick white in winter for camouflage. Has a compact body to retain heat.

animals.name: Reindeer (Caribou)
animals.how_it_survives: Has wide, scoop-like hooves to walk easily on snow and dig down to eat buried lichen.

animals.name: Snowy owl
animals.how_it_survives: Its thick white feathers provide perfect camouflage against the snow and keep it warm in freezing winds.

title: Subnivian Snow Caves
description: Small, hidden caves carved out within deep snow drifts resting on top of the sea ice.
climate: Insulated microclimate (a small, unique climate zone). While the air outside may be -40°C, inside the snow cave it stays close to 0°C.
plants: None inside the cave, but the surrounding ecosystem relies on phytoplankton (tiny aquatic plants) beneath the ice.
fun_facts: Ringed seals carve out these caves using the sharp claws on their front flippers, keeping their pups hidden from polar bears.
Snow is actually an excellent blanket. Because it traps lots of air, it stops the freezing winter wind from reaching the animals huddled inside.
image_caption: A Ringed Seal (Pusa hispida) in its natural habitat: Subnivian Snow Caves.

animals.name: Ringed Seal (Pusa hispida)
animals.how_it_survives: Uses strong claws on its front flippers to hollow out a den (lair) inside the snowdrift to safely hide its pup from polar bears.

animals.name: Stoat (Ermine)
animals.how_it_survives: Changes its brown summer coat to pure white in winter for camouflage while hunting in the snow.

animals.name: Snow vole
animals.how_it_survives: Builds extensive tunnel networks under the snowpack to find roots and stay hidden from owls.

title: Arctic Ocean Pack Ice
description: The freezing, ice-choked waters beneath the surface of the Arctic.
climate: Frigid waters that are often covered by sea ice. Water temperatures hover around -1.8°C (the freezing point of saltwater).
plants: Phytoplankton (microscopic floating plants) and kelp forests in shallower, ice-free zones.
fun_facts: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world's oceans, but it holds a massive amount of the world's fresh water in the form of ice.
The narwhal's famous 'tusk' is actually a giant, spiraled tooth that has millions of nerve endings to help it sense the ocean water.
image_caption: A Narwhal (Monodon monoceros) in its natural habitat: Arctic Ocean Pack Ice.

animals.name: Narwhal (Monodon monoceros)
animals.how_it_survives: Has no dorsal fin on its back, allowing it to swim smoothly just below the thick ice without getting stuck.

animals.name: Narwhal
animals.how_it_survives: Uses its long tusk as a highly sensitive sensory organ to navigate and find food in freezing, dark waters.

animals.name: Beluga whale
animals.how_it_survives: Lacks a dorsal fin on its back, allowing it to swim smoothly right up against the underside of the ice sheets.

title: Open Tundra Mounds
description: Slightly raised bumps on the flat tundra that get blown clear of snow by the harsh winds.
climate: Harsh, windswept, and exposed to extreme cold.
plants: Hardy lichens, mosses, and low-lying arctic willow.
fun_facts: These raised mounds offer a strategic vantage point for predators like the snowy owl to spot prey miles away across the flat tundra.
Because there are no tall trees in the Arctic, a mound just a few feet high is the equivalent of a skyscraper for an owl looking for its dinner.
image_caption: A Snowy Owl (Bubo scandiacus) in its natural habitat: Open Tundra Mounds.

animals.name: Snowy Owl (Bubo scandiacus)
animals.how_it_survives: Nests on the bare ground of these raised mounds, giving it a clear 360-degree view to spot predators and hunt lemmings.

animals.name: Arctic hare
animals.how_it_survives: Has heavily padded, large hind legs for running fast over snow to escape predators without sinking.

animals.name: Ptarmigan
animals.how_it_survives: A hardy bird with heavily feathered feet that act exactly like snowshoes in deep winter snow.

title: Sandy Desert
description: A hot, dry environment covered in shifting sand dunes with very little water.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Hot and cold areas of the world

climate: Hyper-arid (extremely dry) with extreme temperature fluctuations. Scorching hot during the day and freezing cold at night.
plants: Sparse, drought-resistant shrubs and grasses with deep taproots.
fun_facts: The sand in these deserts can heat up to over 70°C (158°F) during the day, forcing animals to adapt unique ways to avoid burning their feet.
The Fennec Fox uses its giant ears not just for hearing insects underground, but like giant radiators to release body heat into the air.
image_caption: A Fennec Fox (Vulpes zerda) in its natural habitat: Sandy Desert.

animals.name: Fennec Fox (Vulpes zerda)
animals.how_it_survives: Has enormous ears that act like radiators to let body heat escape, and fur on the bottom of its paws to protect them from scorching sand.

animals.name: Fennec fox
animals.how_it_survives: Has huge ears that act like radiators to release body heat, and help it listen for prey moving underground.

animals.name: Sandfish skink
animals.how_it_survives: A smooth lizard that can literally 'swim' through loose sand to escape the hot sun and hide.

title: Deep Desert Dunes
description: Vast oceans of sand where food and water might be days of travel apart.
climate: Extremely hot and dry, characterized by shifting sands driven by powerful winds.
plants: Almost non-existent on the dunes themselves due to the constantly shifting sand.
fun_facts: Some massive sand dunes can 'sing' or 'boom' as sand avalanches down their steep faces, creating a low, rumbling sound.
A camel can drink up to 40 gallons of water in one go, and its hump is full of fat, giving it energy for weeks when there is no food.
image_caption: A Dromedary Camel (Camelus dromedarius) in its natural habitat: Deep Desert Dunes.

animals.name: Dromedary Camel (Camelus dromedarius)
animals.how_it_survives: Stores fat (not water) in its hump to survive long journeys. Has long eyelashes and closing nostrils to keep out blowing sand.

animals.name: Namib Desert beetle
animals.how_it_survives: Stands on its head to collect morning fog on its bumpy back, which drips down to its mouth as drinking water.

animals.name: Arabian oryx
animals.how_it_survives: Has a bright white coat to reflect the intense sun and wide hooves for walking on soft sand dunes.

title: Australian Desert Scrub
description: Dry, hot outback terrain with sparse, tough vegetation and red sandy soil.
climate: Arid and hot, but with slightly more moisture than deep sand deserts, allowing for some vegetation.
plants: Spinifex grass, mulga trees, and saltbush.
fun_facts: Many plants in the desert scrub have silvery or pale leaves to reflect the intense sunlight and reduce water loss.
The Thorny Devil looks terrifying, but those spikes are actually used to channel tiny drops of morning dew straight into its mouth!
image_caption: A Thorny Devil (Moloch horridus) in its natural habitat: Australian Desert Scrub.

animals.name: Thorny Devil (Moloch horridus)
animals.how_it_survives: Covered in spikes that collect tiny drops of morning dew. The water then travels through microscopic grooves straight to its mouth.

animals.name: Kangaroo rat
animals.how_it_survives: Never needs to drink liquid water; it gets all the moisture it needs to survive from dry seeds.

animals.name: Roadrunner
animals.how_it_survives: A fast-running bird that is quick enough to hunt and eat venomous snakes and scorpions in the scrubland.

title: Hot Desert Sands
description: Loose sand that gets dangerously hot during the daytime.
climate: Hot desert climate with loose, wind-blown sand that makes movement difficult.
plants: Creosote bush and brittlebush scattered sparsely.
fun_facts: The unique 'sidewinding' motion of some desert snakes keeps only two points of their body touching the hot sand at any time, preventing burns.
Sidewinders can bury themselves in the sand with just their eyes poking out, perfectly camouflaged to ambush lizards.
image_caption: A Sidewinder Rattlesnake (Crotalus cerastes) in its natural habitat: Hot Desert Sands.

animals.name: Sidewinder Rattlesnake (Crotalus cerastes)
animals.how_it_survives: Moves in a unique sideways motion (J-shape) so only two small points of its body touch the burning sand at any one time.

animals.name: Fringe-toed lizard
animals.how_it_survives: Has scale 'fringes' on its toes that let it run quickly across loose, scorching sand without sinking in.

animals.name: Antlion
animals.how_it_survives: Digs clever pitfall traps in the loose sand to catch unwary insects that slip down the sides.

title: Desert Burrows
description: Deep underground tunnels dug into the desert soil where temperatures are cooler.
climate: A microclimate that provides refuge from the extreme desert surface. It stays relatively cool during summer days and warm during winter nights.
plants: Joshua trees, cacti, and desert wildflowers above ground.
fun_facts: A single desert tortoise burrow can be shared by up to 25 other species, including owls, snakes, and lizards, acting as a vital desert oasis (commensalism).
Desert tortoises can feel when it's going to rain and will dig small catch-basins outside their burrows to collect drinking water.
image_caption: A Desert Tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) in its natural habitat: Desert Burrows.

animals.name: Desert Tortoise (Gopherus agassizii)
animals.how_it_survives: Spends up to 95% of its life underground to escape extreme heat. Can store a large amount of water in its bladder for months.

animals.name: Gila monster
animals.how_it_survives: Spends over 90% of its life hidden in cool underground burrows to escape the extreme desert heat.

animals.name: Desert tarantula
animals.how_it_survives: Lines its deep burrow with silk to keep the walls stable and maintain a cool, humid microclimate.

title: Rainforest Canopy
description: The dense, leafy roof of a tropical rainforest, towering up to 30 metres above the ground. It is bathed in sunlight and heavy rain.
climate: Hot, very humid, and wet all year round. The canopy gets the most sunlight and the heaviest rainfall of the entire forest.
plants: Towering trees with wide, umbrella-like branches, heavily draped in lianas (vines) and epiphytes (plants growing on branches) like orchids and bromeliads.
fun_facts: The rainforest canopy is so crowded with life that over 50% of all plant and animal species on Earth live in this one layer!
Sloths are so adapted to hanging upside down in the canopy that their organs are attached to their rib cage so they don't crush their lungs.
image_caption: A Three-toed Sloth (Bradypus) in its natural habitat: Rainforest Canopy.

animals.name: Three-toed Sloth (Bradypus)
animals.how_it_survives: Moves incredibly slowly to avoid being seen by eagles. Its fur even grows green algae, providing perfect camouflage among the leaves.

animals.name: Scarlet macaw
animals.how_it_survives: Uses its incredibly powerful, curved beak to crack open hard rainforest nuts and seeds that other animals can't eat.

animals.name: Spider monkey
animals.how_it_survives: Has a prehensile (gripping) tail that acts like a fifth hand for swinging safely through the high branches.

title: Tropical Coral Reef
description: Vibrant, bustling underwater cities made entirely of limestone skeletons secreted by tiny coral polyps over thousands of years.
climate: Warm, shallow, clear, and sunlit waters, usually between 20°C and 28°C.
plants: Zooxanthellae (microscopic algae living inside the corals) and seaweeds.
fun_facts: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor, but they are home to 25% of all marine species!
Because corals need sunlight for their algae to make food, you will only ever find coral reefs in shallow, clear water.
image_caption: A Clownfish (Amphiprioninae) in its natural habitat: Tropical Coral Reef.

animals.name: Clownfish (Amphiprioninae)
animals.how_it_survives: Develops a thick layer of mucus on its skin to protect it from the stinging tentacles of the sea anemone, giving it a safe, hidden home (commensalism).

animals.name: Parrotfish
animals.how_it_survives: Uses its beak-like teeth to scrape algae off coral. It digests the algae and poops out the coral as fine white sand!

animals.name: Moray eel
animals.how_it_survives: Hides its long body inside narrow coral crevices, waiting to ambush passing prey with its sharp teeth.

title: Deep Sea Abyssal Zone
description: The pitch-black, freezing depths of the ocean floor, miles below the surface where the pressure is intense enough to crush a submarine.
climate: Pitch black, freezing cold (around 2°C), and under immense, crushing water pressure.
plants: No plants can grow here because there is absolutely zero sunlight for photosynthesis. Everything relies on 'marine snow' (dead things falling from above).
fun_facts: The pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench is over 1,000 times the normal atmospheric pressure at sea level.
Because food is so incredibly rare in the deep sea, the anglerfish has an expandable stomach to swallow prey twice its own size!
image_caption: A Anglerfish (Lophiiformes) in its natural habitat: Deep Sea Abyssal Zone.

animals.name: Anglerfish (Lophiiformes)
animals.how_it_survives: Uses a glowing lure on its head (created by bioluminescent bacteria) to attract curious prey straight into its massive, sharp-toothed mouth in the dark.

animals.name: Giant isopod
animals.how_it_survives: A deep-sea scavenger with a rigid, tough exoskeleton to survive the immense crushing pressure of the abyss.

animals.name: Vampire squid
animals.how_it_survives: Can turn itself inside out to display frightening spines and release glowing mucus to confuse predators in the dark.

title: African Savanna
description: Vast, sweeping plains of tall grasses dotted with isolated trees and shrubs, experiencing dramatic wet and dry seasons.
climate: Warm year-round, with a long, brutal dry season where waterholes dry up, followed by a short, intense rainy season.
plants: Tough grasses (like Rhodes grass) and drought-resistant trees like the Baobab and Acacia.
fun_facts: Savannas are shaped by giant herbivores! Elephants constantly knock down trees, which stops the savanna from turning into a dense forest.
During the dry season, millions of wildebeest, zebras, and gazelles travel hundreds of miles together in the 'Great Migration' just to find fresh grass.

curriculum_links.subject: Geography
curriculum_links.topic: Hot and cold areas of the world

image_caption: A Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) in its natural habitat: African Savanna.

animals.name: Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus)
animals.how_it_survives: Evolved a flexible spine and non-retractable claws (like football boots) for immense grip, making it the fastest land animal to sprint across the open plains.

animals.name: Giraffe
animals.how_it_survives: Has a uniquely long neck to reach nutritious leaves on tall acacia trees that grazing animals below cannot reach.

animals.name: African elephant
animals.how_it_survives: Flaps its giant ears to cool its blood, and uses its trunk to dig for water during the dry season.

title: High Alpine Peaks
description: The rugged, rocky, and steep slopes of mountains above the 'tree line', where the air is thin and the weather is unpredictable.
climate: Very cold and windy with thin air (less oxygen). It gets much colder the higher up the mountain you climb.
plants: Alpine cushion plants, mosses, and tough grasses that grow low to the ground to avoid the fierce winds. No trees can survive up here.
fun_facts: The paws of a snow leopard are extremely wide and act like natural snowshoes, stopping them from sinking into deep drifts.
Unlike most big cats, snow leopards cannot roar. Instead, they make a non-aggressive puffing sound called a 'chuff'.
image_caption: A Snow Leopard (Panthera uncia) in its natural habitat: High Alpine Peaks.

animals.name: Snow Leopard (Panthera uncia)
animals.how_it_survives: Has a giant, thick tail nearly a metre long, which it wraps around its face like a scarf to stay warm while sleeping on freezing rocky ledges.

animals.name: Alpine ibex
animals.how_it_survives: Has specialized cloven hooves with soft, rubbery pads that grip sheer, nearly vertical rock faces.

animals.name: Himalayan monal
animals.how_it_survives: A hardy bird that uses its strong curved beak to dig through mountain snow to find buried roots and seeds.

title: River
description: A flowing body of freshwater that journeys from high ground all the way to the sea.
climate: Temperate, with water temperatures changing with the seasons and water levels rising rapidly after heavy rain.
plants: Water crowfoot, trailing willow branches on the banks, and tall reeds that provide shelter.
fun_facts: Rivers act as wildlife highways, allowing animals to travel safely and unseen across the country.
The faster the water flows, the more oxygen it traps, which is why some fish like salmon only live in fast rapids!
image_caption: An Otter (Lutra lutra) in its natural habitat: River.

animals.name: Eurasian Otter
animals.how_it_survives: Has webbed feet for powerful swimming, dense waterproof fur, and can close its ears and nose underwater while hunting for fish.

animals.name: Kingfisher
animals.how_it_survives: A bird with a streamlined, bullet-shaped body that lets it dive into the water without making a splash to catch small fish.

animals.name: Atlantic Salmon
animals.how_it_survives: Born in the river, swims out to the ocean to grow, and then uses a magnetic sense to find its exact birth river to lay its own eggs!

title: Rock Pool
description: Small pools of seawater left behind in the rocks on the beach when the tide goes out.
climate: Extreme microclimate! It can get very hot and salty in the summer sun, or freezing cold in the winter wind before the tide returns.
plants: Tough seaweeds like kelp, bladderwrack, and encrusting pink algae that cling tightly to the rocks.
fun_facts: Animals in a rock pool must survive being baked by the sun, battered by crashing waves, and hunted by seagulls all in one day!
Limpets have teeth made of the strongest biological material ever tested—stronger than spider silk!
image_caption: A Shore Crab (Carcinus maenas) in its natural habitat: Rock Pool.

animals.name: Shore Crab
animals.how_it_survives: Has a tough exoskeleton to protect it from waves and predators, and hides deep in the rocky crevices when the tide is out.

animals.name: Common Limpet
animals.how_it_survives: Clamps down onto the rock with incredible force, sealing water inside its shell to stop itself from drying out in the sun.

animals.name: Beadlet Anemone
animals.how_it_survives: Pulls its stinging tentacles inside its body when the tide goes out, looking like a harmless blob of red jelly to conserve moisture.

title: Taiga Forest
description: The largest land habitat on Earth, made up of endless evergreen coniferous trees stretching across the cold north.
climate: Subarctic. Long, freezing winters with heavy snow, and very short, mild summers.
plants: Conifer trees like pine, spruce, and fir, which keep their needle-like leaves all year round to catch the weak winter sun.
fun_facts: The Taiga is so massive that it stretches all the way across North America, Europe, and Asia, holding nearly a third of all the trees in the world!
Conifer needles have a thick waxy coating to stop them from freezing and drying out in the bitter winter wind.
image_caption: A Brown Bear (Ursus arctos) in its natural habitat: Taiga Forest.

animals.name: Brown Bear
animals.how_it_survives: Eats heavily during the short summer to build up fat, then hibernates in a den through the freezing winter when food is scarce.

animals.name: Moose (Elk)
animals.how_it_survives: Has incredibly long legs to wade through deep winter snow and reach the high branches of pine trees.

animals.name: Pine Marten
animals.how_it_survives: An agile tree-climber with semi-retractable claws, allowing it to leap between snow-covered branches to hunt red squirrels.

title: Urban Garden
description: A man-made habitat full of fences, lawns, and flowerbeds that provides a surprising haven for wildlife in the middle of a city.
climate: Temperate, but often slightly warmer than the surrounding countryside because city buildings trap the sun's heat (the 'urban heat island' effect).
plants: A mix of native weeds (like dandelions), planted ornamental flowers, lawn grass, and climbing ivy on fences.
fun_facts: There are over 20 million gardens in the UK. If you put them all together, they would be a bigger habitat than all of the UK's nature reserves combined!
Many animals have learned that human gardens are great places to find food, from bird feeders to compost bins.
image_caption: An Urban Fox (Vulpes vulpes) in its natural habitat: Urban Garden.

animals.name: Urban Fox
animals.how_it_survives: Highly adaptable and not a fussy eater; it will hunt mice, eat fallen fruit, or scavenge leftover takeaways from bins.

animals.name: Hedgehog
animals.how_it_survives: Travels through small holes in fences at night, eating slugs and snails from the flowerbeds to help the gardeners.

animals.name: Garden Spider
animals.how_it_survives: Spins large orb webs across gaps in fences or bushes to catch flying insects, rebuilding the web every single morning.

title: Wildflower Meadow
description: An open, grassy habitat bursting with colourful flowers that relies on traditional farming or grazing to survive.
climate: Temperate, requiring plenty of spring and summer sunshine for the massive variety of flowers to bloom.
plants: A huge variety of native flowers like ox-eye daisies, buttercups, yellow rattle, and red clover, mixed with fine grasses.
fun_facts: A healthy meadow can be home to over 100 different types of flowers, attracting thousands of buzzing pollinators.
Since the 1930s, the UK has lost 97% of its wildflower meadows, making them one of our most threatened and precious habitats.
image_caption: A Buff-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) in its natural habitat: Wildflower Meadow.

animals.name: Buff-tailed Bumblebee
animals.how_it_survives: Covered in thick hair to stay warm while flying from flower to flower, collecting nectar and accidentally pollinating the plants.

animals.name: Meadow Brown Butterfly
animals.how_it_survives: The caterpillars feed exclusively on the fine meadow grasses, perfectly camouflaged in the green stems.

animals.name: Field Vole
animals.how_it_survives: Weaves intricate tunnel networks through the tall grass to safely hunt for seeds without being spotted by birds of prey above.

title: Rainforest Floor
description: The dark, damp bottom layer of the rainforest where giant tree roots spread out and fallen leaves are quickly recycled.
climate: Hot, incredibly humid, and very dark. Less than 2% of the sunlight from the canopy reaches the floor!
plants: Giant buttress roots of canopy trees, shade-loving ferns, and weird fungi that glow in the dark.
fun_facts: Because it is so dark, many plants on the forest floor have giant leaves to catch as much of the tiny amount of sunlight as possible.
If a leaf falls to the rainforest floor, it breaks down and disappears in just 6 weeks because the fungi and bugs work so fast!
image_caption: Leaf-cutter Ants (Atta) in their natural habitat: Rainforest Floor.

animals.name: Leaf-cutter Ant
animals.how_it_survives: Cuts pieces of leaves and carries them underground, using them to farm a special fungus which they then eat.

animals.name: Jaguar
animals.how_it_survives: Has a beautiful spotted coat (rosettes) that provides perfect camouflage in the dappled shadows of the forest floor while stalking prey.

animals.name: Poison Dart Frog
animals.how_it_survives: Uses incredibly bright colours to warn predators on the dark forest floor that its skin is highly toxic.
